strengths: Simple and computationally zero-overhead plug-and-play technique that can be integrated into existing loss functions (Cross-Entropy and Supervised Contrastive) and OSR pipelines.

Intuitive motivation backed by geometric intuition: starting with low temperature enforces instance-level discriminability and coarse separation, while gradually increasing temperature promotes tighter intra-class clusters without pulling unseen open-set samples into known clusters.

Comprehensive evaluation across standard OSR benchmarks and the more realistic Semantic Shift Benchmarks (SSBs: CUB, FGVC-Aircraft, Stanford Cars), comparing against constant temperatures, reverse temperature schedules (CosSch), and other schedules.
weaknesses: The technical contribution is relatively incremental, essentially consisting of an inverted cosine schedule for the loss temperature parameter during training.

Performance improvements on standard OSR benchmarks (CIFAR-10, CIFAR+10, CIFAR+50, TinyImageNet) are very marginal and often within the margin of error (e.g., in Table 1, CIFAR+10 drops from 97.90% to 97.88% and CIFAR+50 drops from 96.50% to 96.32% for CE; Table 3 shows standard deviations between 0.5% and 3.4%, overshadowing the 0.05%–0.2% gains).

Inconsistency across settings on SSBs: for instance, on FGVC-Aircraft with SupCon + Label Smoothing (Table 2), the proposed method degrades performance compared to the baseline (AUROC drops from 86.94/81.40 to 85.36/81.29).

Sensitivity and search overhead for the new hyperparameters $(\tau^-, \tau^+, P)$: while the method itself adds no runtime overhead, tuning the scheduling range requires additional empirical exploration compared to a single temperature parameter.

strengths: The method is computationally lightweight and can be easily plugged into existing training pipelines utilizing cross-entropy or supervised contrastive losses without adding architectural complexity or inference latency.

The authors evaluate the approach across a wide set of benchmarks, including standard small-scale datasets (CIFAR-10, CIFAR+10, CIFAR+50, TinyImageNet) and Semantic Shift Benchmarks (CUB, FGVC-Aircraft, Stanford Cars).
The manuscript provides helpful qualitative representations (UMAP plots) to illustrate the intuition behind instance vs. semantic clustering across different temperature values.
weaknesses: The core technical contribution is very limited in novelty. Shifting or inverting the phase of an established cosine scheduler (as used in Kukleva et al., 2023) for a scalar hyperparameter is an incremental heuristic rather than a substantive algorithmic innovation.

Performance improvements on standard benchmarks are marginal and within statistical noise. For instance, in Table 1, the AUROC changes from 93.6% to 93.76% on CIFAR-10 and remains identical at 97.03% on CIFAR+50. Looking at Table 3, the standard deviations across splits (ranging from 0.20% to 2.10%) dwarf many of the reported gains, suggesting the improvements are not statistically significant.

The method introduces additional hyperparameters (upper temperature tau+, lower temperature tau-, period P, and phase shift k). It is unclear how much of the performance gain stems from extensive tuning of the temperature bounds rather than the negative cosine trajectory itself.

The experimental setup for contrastive learning on the Semantic Shift Benchmarks is suboptimal. Due to hardware constraints (a single RTX 2080Ti), the batch size for SupCon was set to 12. Contrastive learning methods (especially SupCon) degrade severely with very small batch sizes because each batch contains insufficient positive and negative pairs. This likely explains why CE consistently outperforms SupCon on SSBs in Table 2, weakening the empirical claims made about contrastive representation learning.

The theoretical backing for why starting cold and ending warm is beneficial remains purely speculative and heuristic. The manuscript offers intuitive arguments about neighbor prioritization and decision boundary smoothing, but lacks rigorous mathematical or gradient-level justification.

strengths: Simple, lightweight, and plug-and-play: The proposed negative cosine temperature scheduling (NegCosSch) requires virtually no additional computational or memory overhead, making it easily adoptable into standard cross-entropy and supervised contrastive loss pipelines.

Intuitive motivation supported by visualizations: The paper provides a clear intuitive rationale—starting with lower temperatures to establish separation boundaries via hard instance discrimination, then warming up to higher temperatures to smooth representations and enhance intra-class compactness—which is qualitatively supported by UMAP trajectories.

Thorough evaluation on challenging Semantic Shift Benchmarks (SSBs): Unlike many recent OSR works that restrict evaluations to small toy splits, this work thoroughly evaluates on fine-grained semantic benchmarks (CUB, FGVC-Aircraft, Stanford Cars) across Accuracy, AUROC, and OSCR metrics.

Comprehensive scheduling ablations: The comparison in Table 4 evaluates alternative schedules (random, step-up, phase shifts $k$, half-cosine), clearly showing why the inverted cosine wave with a sustained final temperature performs best.
weaknesses: Marginal improvements on standard OSR benchmarks: As shown in Table 1 and Table 3, performance gains on standard benchmarks (CIFAR-10, CIFAR+10, CIFAR+50) are minimal (often within $\le 0.1-0.2\%$ AUROC) and fall well within the reported standard deviation intervals.

Increased hyperparameter search space: Replacing a single scalar temperature $\tau$ with a schedule introduces multiple parameters $(\tau^-, \tau^+, P, k)$. While general heuristic ranges are suggested (e.g., perturbing around optimal constant $\tau$), sensitivity analysis across different architectures and domains remains somewhat limited.

Lack of formal theoretical analysis: The rationale relies mostly on empirical observations and qualitative geometric arguments; a deeper theoretical investigation of the gradient dynamics under shifting temperature scales in classification/contrastive losses would significantly strengthen the paper.

Baseline comparability nuance on SSBs: Due to the unavailability of the original checkpoint used by Vaze et al. [2022], a different Places365 pretrained model was used, which slightly complicates direct numerical comparison with prior published numbers, although the authors appropriately re-ran baseline counterparts under identical settings.

strengths: The paper is well-motivated and addresses a practical problem in Open Set Recognition (OSR) with a simple, zero-parameter-overhead plug-and-play technique (temperature scheduling).

The core empirical observation—that starting with a low temperature and increasing it (the 'negative cosine' or monotonic increase schedule) outperforms traditional temperature cool-down schedules—is novel, counter-intuitive, and well-contextualized within representation learning trade-offs.

Comprehensive experimental evaluation across multiple losses (Cross-Entropy, Supervised Contrastive, ARPL, and Prototypical Contrastive), architectures (VGG, ResNet, Vision Transformer), and benchmarks, especially the challenging Semantic Shift Benchmarks (SSBs).
Thorough ablation studies and variance reporting across five random seeds, providing clear insight into hyperparameter selection for temperature bounds and period lengths.
weaknesses: The technical novelty is somewhat incremental, as the proposed method primarily consists of scheduling an existing scalar hyperparameter (temperature) using inverted cosine or monotonic functions.

The performance improvements on several standard benchmarks (e.g., TinyImageNet in Table 1 and CIFAR-10/CIFAR+10/CIFAR+50 in Table 9) are marginal or within the margin of standard deviation, indicating that the benefits may be primarily confined to fine-grained semantic shift regimes.
The theoretical justification relies mainly on heuristic gradient inspections rather than formal bounds or rigorous geometric proofs regarding open-space risk or feature collapse.
The method introduces additional hyperparameters $(\tau^-, \tau^+)$ that require empirical tuning, although heuristic rules of thumb are suggested.

strengths: Practicality and zero computational overhead: The proposed temperature scheduling strategy is lightweight, requiring only a few lines of code to modulate temperature during training without needing additional models, data synthesis, or auxiliary optimization objectives.

Comprehensive empirical validation across diverse loss functions and architectures: The method is validated on standard cross-entropy, supervised contrastive learning (SupCon), adversarial reciprocal point learning (ARPL), and prototypical contrastive learning across multiple architectures (VGG, ResNet-50, and Tiny-ViT).

Adherence to rigorous modern OSR evaluation protocols: The paper properly evaluates on the Semantic Shift Benchmarks (SSBs: CUB, Aircraft, Stanford Cars) with both 'Easy' and 'Hard' splits, and reports multi-seed standard deviations, closed-set accuracy, AUROC, and OSCR.

Thorough comparison among scheduling dynamics: The ablation in Table 1 effectively compares various shapes (linear decrease/increase, random, logarithmic, exponential, standard cosine, and negative cosine), providing clear empirical evidence that an increasing temperature trajectory consistently outperforms constant or decreasing schedules.
weaknesses: Limited conceptual novelty and theoretical depth: The core algorithmic contribution consists of applying a reversed/monotonic temperature schedule (low-to-high) to existing loss functions, adapting insights from prior contrastive learning literature (e.g., Wang & Liu 2021, Kukleva et al. 2023). The explanation is largely heuristic and qualitative, lacking a formal theoretical framework to explain why representations retain early instance-level separation when temperature is subsequently increased.

Marginal gains on coarse/standard benchmarks: On standard coarse benchmarks such as CIFAR-10, CIFAR+10, CIFAR+50 (Table 9), and TinyImageNet (Table 2), the performance gains over well-tuned constant temperature baselines are modest (often < 0.3% - 0.6% AUROC), indicating that the primary advantages are concentrated in fine-grained transfer scenarios.

Hyperparameter expansion: While the authors propose empirical heuristics for setting (tau_plus, tau_minus), the approach introduces two temperature bounds (and a period parameter P for periodic variants) in place of a single scalar temperature, requiring careful range selection across different loss types.

strengths: Simplicity and zero computational overhead: The proposed temperature modulation can be incorporated into standard loss functions (Cross-Entropy, Supervised Contrastive, ARPL) by modifying only the epoch-dependent temperature parameter, requiring no extra memory, auxiliary generation, or training time.

Rigorous experimental protocol: The paper evaluates on the challenging Semantic Shift Benchmarks (SSBs: CUB, FGVC-Aircraft, Stanford Cars) following established competitive baselines (Vaze et al., 2022), reporting both 'Easy' and 'Hard' splits along with standard deviations over multiple runs.

Broad empirical coverage: The authors validate the schedule across multiple loss formulations (CE, SupCon, ARPL, ProtoCon), architectures (ResNet-50, VGG, ViT), and provide ablations comparing multiple schedule shapes (linear, exponential, periodic, and monotonic).
weaknesses: Limited conceptual novelty: The core contribution is scheduling the temperature parameter during training by starting low and ending high (an inverted/negative cosine schedule or monotonic increase). Temperature scheduling and annealing have been extensively explored in contrastive learning, self-supervised learning, and language modeling (e.g., Kukleva et al., 2023; Wang & Liu, 2021).

Over-emphasis on the specific cosine formulation: In the ablation studies (Table 1), simple monotonic schedules (such as a standard linear increase) perform essentially on par with the proposed NegCosSch across nearly all benchmarks and metrics (e.g., AUROC Hard on CUB: 78.01% for Linear vs. 78.08% for M-NegCosSch; SCars: 86.18% vs. 86.26%). This indicates that the specific functional form of NegCosSch provides negligible advantage over trivial monotonic warming.

Marginal gains on several standard datasets: While notable gains are observed on CUB and Aircraft, the improvements on TinyImageNet and the CIFAR benchmarks (Table 9) are minimal to negligible (e.g., CIFAR10 AUROC moves from 94.04% to 94.10%, and CIFAR+50 remains identical at 97.03%), which often fall within standard error.

Heuristic and qualitative justification: The rationale linking temperature trajectories to open-set feature clustering relies entirely on intuitive interpretations of contrastive gradients from prior literature, lacking formal theoretical analysis or deep mechanistic verification of why this trajectory inherently protects open-set representations from collapsing near known decision boundaries.

Fairness of constant baselines: The constant baseline for Cross-Entropy is restricted to $\tau=1.0$ in main tables, while the proposed schedule navigates a broader dynamic range. It remains unclear whether simply finding a slightly higher fixed constant temperature (or standard post-hoc logit scaling) would close a significant portion of the observed performance gap.
